label: thm:glauber-odd-k-informal
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:glauber-odd-k-informal}
Let $k\geqslant3$ be odd, and let $H(x)\doteq N^{-\tfrac{k-1}{2}}\left\langle Y, x^{\otimes k} \right\rangle$ denote the tensor PCA Hamiltonian with $\lambda\gtrsim\lambda_{\mathrm{ALG}}$. Then, with a uniformly random initialization and suitable inverse temperatures, \cref{alg:averaged-annealed-glauber} run with $T_{\mathrm{av}}\gtrsim N^{2k+o(1)}$ and $\log N\lesssim T\lesssim\operatorname{poly}(N)$ strongly recovers the planted signal with probability at least $1-\exp(-N^{1/2-o(1)})$.

label: lem:discrete-product-rule
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Discrete product rule

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply the coordinate flip identity to $f$, $g$, and $fg$ to obtain
\begin{align*}
    2x_i\partial_i(fg)(x)
    &=f(x)g(x)-f(x^{\sim i})g(x^{\sim i})\\
    &=f(x)g(x)
    -\bigl(f(x)-2x_i\partial_i f(x)\bigr)
     \bigl(g(x)-2x_i\partial_i g(x)\bigr)\\
    &=2x_i\bigl(f(x)\partial_i g(x)+g(x)\partial_i f(x)\bigr)
      -4\partial_i f(x)\partial_i g(x).
\end{align*}

Dividing by $2x_i$ and using $x_i^2=1$, we obtain the desired identity.

label: lem:commutants-bn
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:commutants-bn}
Any matrix that commutes with every element of $O(N,\mathbb Z)$ must be a scalar multiple of the identity.
head: environment
name: Commutants of $O(N,\Z)$

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}$ satisfy $AM=MA$ for every $M\in O(N,\mathbb Z)$. Consider distinct $i,j\in[N]$, and let $D$ be a diagonal sign matrix with $D_{ii}=+1$ and $D_{jj}=-1$. Since $D\in O(N,\mathbb Z)$, we have $AD=DA$, and hence
\begin{align*}
    (AD)_{ij}=A_{ij}D_{jj}=-A_{ij},
    \qquad
    (DA)_{ij}=D_{ii}A_{ij}=A_{ij}.
\end{align*}
It follows that $A_{ij}=0$ for $i\ne j$, so $A=\operatorname{diag}(a)$ for some $a\in\mathbb{R}^N$. Now let $P$ be the permutation matrix that exchanges coordinates $i$ and $j$. Since $P\in O(N,\mathbb Z)$, we have $A=PAP^\top$, and therefore $a_i=a_j$. Thus $a_1=\cdots=a_N$ and $A=cI$ for some $c\in\mathbb{R}$.

label: rem:average-gradient-snr
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:average-gradient-snr}
We make the following observations from \cref{avg-discrete-grad-snr}. For even $k$, spin flip symmetry forces $u_H=0$, so the average discrete gradient carries no information about the planted signal. For odd $k$, it is a noisy observation of the planted vector $x^{\star}$, with signal-to-noise ratio $\lambda\sigma_N\asymp_k\lambda N^{-\tfrac{k-1}{4}}$. In particular, at the conjectured algorithmic threshold $\lambda\gtrsim_k N^{\tfrac{k-2}{4}}$, the SNR is at least $\Omega(N^{-\nicefrac{1}{4}})$. This is formalized in the following corollary.
head: environment

label: cor:avg-discrete-grad-correlation
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Correlation of the Sign-Rounded Average Discrete Gradient

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cref{avg-discrete-grad-snr} and the identity $\sigma_N^2=\alpha_N\sqrt N$, we have $u_H=\lambda\sigma_N^2x^{\star}+\zeta$, where $\zeta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_N^2I)$. Let $t_N=\lambda\sigma_N$ and $Z_i=\tfrac{x^{\star}_i\zeta_i}{\sigma_N}$. Then $Z_1,\ldots,Z_N\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, and the signed coordinates $Y_i=x^{\star}_i(\widehat u_H)_i$ satisfy, almost surely,
\begin{align*}
    Y_i
    =x^{\star}_i\operatorname{sgn}\left(\lambda\sigma_N^2x^{\star}_i+\zeta_i\right)
    =\operatorname{sgn}\left(\lambda\sigma_N^2+x^{\star}_i\zeta_i\right)
    =\operatorname{sgn}(t_N+Z_i).
\end{align*}
Consequently, the $Y_i$ are i.i.d. biased Rademacher variables and $m(\widehat u_H)=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i$.

We first bound their common mean. By symmetry of the standard Gaussian density,
\begin{align*}
    \mu_N\doteq\mathbb{E}[Y_i]
    &=\mathbb{P}[Z_i\geqslant-t_N]-\mathbb{P}[Z_i<-t_N]
    =2\mathbb{P}[0\leqslant Z_i\leqslant t_N]\\
    &=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\int_0^{t_N}e^{-\tfrac{s^2}{2}}\,ds
    \geqslant\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi e}}\min\{t_N,1\},
\end{align*}
where we restrict the integral to $[0,\min\{t_N,1\}]$ and use $e^{-\tfrac{s^2}{2}}\geqslant e^{-\nicefrac{1}{2}}$ on $[0,1]$. Similarly, bounding the Gaussian density by $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}$ and using $\mu_N\leqslant1$, we obtain $\mu_N\leqslant\min\{t_N,1\}$. Moreover, Since the $Y_i$ are i.i.d. biased Rademacher variables with mean $\mu_N$, we obtain the following via a Chernoff bound \citep{van2014probability}:
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{P}\left[\left|m(\widehat u_H)-\mu_N\right|\geqslant\frac{\mu_N}{2}\right]
    \leqslant2\exp\left(-\frac{N\mu_N^2}{8}\right)
    \leqslant2\exp\left(-cN\min\{t_N^2,1\}\right).
\end{align*}
The first claim follows by applying $c_k\min\{t_N,1\}\leqslant\mu_N\leqslant\min\{t_N,1\}$ with $t_N=\lambda\sigma_N\asymp_k\lambda N^{-\tfrac{k-1}{4}}$ and adjusting constants appropriately.

Finally, if $\lambda\geqslant C_kN^{\tfrac{k-2}{4}}$, then $\lambda N^{-\tfrac{k-1}{4}}\geqslant C_kN^{-\nicefrac{1}{4}}$ and $\lambda^2N^{-\tfrac{k-3}{2}}\geqslant C_k^2\sqrt N$. The second claim then follows for sufficiently large $N$ by adjusting constants appropriately.

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:average-hessian-snr}
For even $k$, we observe from \cref{avg-discrete-hess-snr} that the rank $1$ spike in the average discrete Hessian is precisely $\theta^{\star}$. Indeed, $A_{\mathrm{sig}}$ has top eigenvector $\theta^{\star}$ and eigengap $\lambda_1(A_{\mathrm{sig}})-\lambda_2(A_{\mathrm{sig}})=\lambda\gamma_N$. Relative to the noise scale $\sqrt{\gamma_N}$, the signal-to-noise ratio is therefore $\lambda\sqrt{\gamma_N}\asymp_k\lambda N^{-\tfrac{k-2}{4}}$. Hence, the Davis--Kahan theorem \citep[Theorem~4.5.5]{vershynin2018high} suggests that a top unit eigenvector of $A_H$ achieves constant absolute correlation with $\theta^{\star}$ with probability at least $1-\exp(-cN)$ whenever $\lambda$ is above the conjectured algorithmic threshold, namely when $\lambda\gtrsim N^{\tfrac{k-2}{4}}$

\label{rem:srw-green-operator-provenance}
By \cref{eq:srw-poisson-equation}, we may interpret $\mathcal{R}$ as the inverse of $-\mathcal{L}$ restricted to $L^2_0(\pi)$. Solutions to the Poisson equation are a canonical tool for proving central limit theorems for ergodic averages of Markov processes~\citep{komorowski2012fluctuations,eberle2025markov} (see also~\citep[Section~4.1]{chatterjee2005concentration} for connections to Stein's method of exchangeable pairs). More recently, such methods have been used to compare stationary distributions of contractive Markov chains under Dobrushin's conditions~\citep{bresler2019stein,reinert2019approximating}. In subsequent sections, we shall use the Green operator to analyze ergodic averages along high-temperature Glauber dynamics for Hamiltonians with bounded $\mathcal{D}^2$ norm.

label: lem:kspin-gaussian-conditioning
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Decomposition of the $k$-Spin Hamiltonian

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cref{lem:hypercube-stein}, $\zeta=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi}[yH_0(y)]$. Hence, for every $x\in\Omega_N$ and $i\in[N]$, we obtain the following from \cref{eq:kspin-covariance} and \cref{eq:average-gradient-variance-moment} in the proof of \cref{avg-discrete-grad-snr}:
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}[H_0(x)\zeta_i]
    &=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi}\bigl[y_i\mathbb{E}[H_0(x)H_0(y)]\bigr]\\
    &=N^{1-k}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi}\left[y_i\left(\sum_{j=1}^Nx_jy_j\right)^k\right]\\
    &=x_iN^{1-k}\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\pi}\left[z_i\left(\sum_{j=1}^Nz_j\right)^k\right]
    =\sigma_N^2x_i,
\end{align*}
where we used the change of variables $z_j=x_jy_j$ and permutation invariance of $\pi$.

Since $k\geqslant3$ is odd, \cref{eq:average-gradient-variance-moment} implies that $\sigma_N^2>0$. As $(H_0(x))_{x\in\Omega_N}$ and $\zeta$ are jointly Gaussian and $\mathbb{E}[\zeta\zeta^\top]=\sigma_N^2I$, the Gaussian conditioning formula~\citep[Theorems~9.1 and~9.9]{janson1997gaussian} implies that $\mathbb{E}[H_0(x)\mid\zeta]=\left\langle \zeta, x \right\rangle$ and that $H_0^\perp(x)\doteq H_0(x)-\left\langle \zeta, x \right\rangle$ is a centered Gaussian process independent of $\zeta$. 
Moreover, we obtain 
\begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}\bigl[H_0^\perp(x)H_0^\perp(y)\bigr]
    &=\mathbb{E}\bigl[(H_0(x)-\left\langle \zeta, x \right\rangle)(H_0(y)-\left\langle \zeta, y \right\rangle)\bigr]\\
    &=\mathbb{E}[H_0(x)H_0(y)]-\sum_{i=1}^Ny_i\mathbb{E}[H_0(x)\zeta_i]-\sum_{i=1}^Nx_i\mathbb{E}[H_0(y)\zeta_i]+\sum_{i,j=1}^Nx_iy_j\mathbb{E}[\zeta_i\zeta_j]\\
    &=N\left(\frac{\left\langle x, y \right\rangle}{N}\right)^k-2\sigma_N^2\sum_{i=1}^Nx_iy_i+\sigma_N^2\sum_{i=1}^Nx_iy_i\\
    &=N\left(\frac{\left\langle x, y \right\rangle}{N}\right)^k-\sigma_N^2\left\langle x, y \right\rangle,
\end{align*}
which concludes the proof.
head: environment

label: lem:tpca-hamiltonian-under-gauge
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Gauge-Transformed Hamiltonian

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $x^{\star}\in\Omega_N$, by direct computation,
\begin{align*}
    m_\phi(y)
    =m(x^{\star}\odot\phi\odot y)
    =\frac{1}{N}\left\langle x^{\star}, x^{\star}\odot\phi\odot y \right\rangle
    =\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N(x^{\star}_i)^2\phi_iy_i
    =\frac{1}{N}\left\langle \phi, y \right\rangle.
\end{align*}
Next, since $u_H=\lambda\sigma_N^2x^{\star}+\zeta$ and $\left\langle x^{\star}, x \right\rangle=Nm(x)$, we infer from \cref{eq:tensor-pca-hamiltonian,lem:kspin-gaussian-conditioning} that
\begin{align*}
    H(x)
    &=N\lambda m(x)^k+\left\langle \zeta, x \right\rangle+H_0^\perp(x)\\
    &=\left\langle u_H, x \right\rangle+N\lambda m(x)^k-N\lambda\sigma_N^2m(x)+H_0^\perp(x).
\end{align*}
Moreover, since $u_H=x^{\star}\odot U$,
\begin{align*}
    \left\langle u_H, x^{\star}\odot\phi\odot y \right\rangle
    =\sum_{i=1}^NU_i\phi_iy_i
    =\sum_{i=1}^NR_iy_i
    =\left\langle R, y \right\rangle.
\end{align*}
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
    H_\phi(y)
    &=H(x^{\star}\odot\phi\odot y)\\
    &=\left\langle R, y \right\rangle+N\lambda m_\phi(y)^k-N\lambda\sigma_N^2m_\phi(y)+H_0^\perp(x^{\star}\odot\phi\odot y)\\
    &=H_{\mathrm{null}}(y)+H_{\mathrm{sig}}(y).
\end{align*}

We next prove the first claim. Since $x^{\star}\in\Omega_N$ is fixed, $(\phi,R)$ is a measurable function of $\zeta$. Moreover, by \cref{lem:kspin-gaussian-conditioning}, $H_0^\perp$ is a centered Gaussian process independent of $\zeta$. Since the map $y\mapstox^{\star}\odot\phi\odot y$ is an isometry of $\Omega_N$ and the covariance of $H_0^\perp$ depends only on $\left\langle x, y \right\rangle$, the law of $H_0^\perp$ is invariant under this transformation. Hence,
\begin{align*}
    \operatorname{Law}(W\mid\phi,R)
    =\operatorname{Law}\bigl(H_0^\perp(x^{\star}\odot\phi\odot\cdot)\mid\phi,R\bigr)
    =\operatorname{Law}(H_0^\perp\mid\phi,R)
    =\operatorname{Law}(H_0^\perp).
\end{align*}
Thus, $W$ is independent of $(\phi,R)$ and has the same law as $H_0^\perp$.

The second claim is a standard consequence of the gauge invariance of Glauber dynamics (see \citep[\S4.10]{nishimori2001statistical} for a proof in the special case of the Edwards--Anderson model). We present a proof below for completeness. Define the gauge transformation operator $\Lambda_\phi:\Omega_N\to\Omega_N$ as $\Lambda_\phi x\doteqx^{\star}\odot\phi\odot x$, and for any $f:\Omega_N\to\mathbb{R}$, define $\Lambda_\phi f\doteq f\circ\Lambda_\phi$. Observe that $\Lambda_\phi^2=I$, that $\Lambda_\phi$ commutes with coordinate flips, i.e., $\Lambda_\phi x^{\sim i}=(\Lambda_\phi x)^{\sim i}$, and that $H_\phi=\Lambda_\phi H$. Recall from \cref{eq:glauber-generator} that the generator of Glauber dynamics for $H$ at inverse temperature $\beta$ is
\begin{align*}
    \mathcal{L}_{H,\beta}F(x)
    =\sum_{i=1}^Nc_i^{(H,\beta)}(x)\bigl[F(x^{\sim i})-F(x)\bigr],
    \qquad
    c_i^{(H,\beta)}(x)
    =\frac12\bigl[1-x_i\tanh(\beta\partial_iH(x))\bigr].
\end{align*}
Since $2x_i\partial_iH(x)=H(x)-H(x^{\sim i})$, the flip rate $c_i^{(H,\beta)}(x)$ depends on $x$ only through $H(x^{\sim i})-H(x)$. Moreover, for any $x\in\Omega_N$,
\begin{align*}
    H_\phi\bigl((\Lambda_\phi x)^{\sim i}\bigr)-H_\phi(\Lambda_\phi x)
    &=H_\phi(\Lambda_\phi x^{\sim i})-H_\phi(\Lambda_\phi x)\\
    &=H(\Lambda_\phi^2x^{\sim i})-H(\Lambda_\phi^2x)
    =H(x^{\sim i})-H(x),
\end{align*}
and hence, $c_i^{(H_\phi,\beta)}(\Lambda_\phi x)=c_i^{(H,\beta)}(x)$. It follows that for any $F:\Omega_N\to\mathbb{R}$,
\begin{align*}
    (\mathcal{L}_{H,\beta}\Lambda_\phi F)(x)
    &=\sum_{i=1}^Nc_i^{(H,\beta)}(x)\bigl[F(\Lambda_\phi x^{\sim i})-F(\Lambda_\phi x)\bigr]\\
    &=\sum_{i=1}^Nc_i^{(H_\phi,\beta)}(\Lambda_\phi x)\bigl[F\bigl((\Lambda_\phi x)^{\sim i}\bigr)-F(\Lambda_\phi x)\bigr]
    =(\Lambda_\phi\mathcal{L}_{H_\phi,\beta}F)(x).
\end{align*}
Hence, $\Lambda_\phi\mathcal{L}_{H,\beta}\Lambda_\phi=\mathcal{L}_{H_\phi,\beta}$. Finally, since $Y_t(e)=\Lambda_\phi X_t(\Lambda_\phi e)$, for any $F:\Omega_N\to\mathbb{R}$,
\begin{align*}
    \left.\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb{E}\bigl[F(Y_t(e))\bigr]\right|_{t=0}
    &=\left.\frac{d}{dt}\mathbb{E}\bigl[F\bigl(\Lambda_\phi X_t(\Lambda_\phi e)\bigr)\bigr]\right|_{t=0}\\
    &=(\mathcal{L}_{H,\beta}\Lambda_\phi F)(\Lambda_\phi e)
    =(\Lambda_\phi\mathcal{L}_{H,\beta}\Lambda_\phi F)(e)
    =(\mathcal{L}_{H_\phi,\beta}F)(e),
\end{align*}
where the expectations are taken with the Hamiltonian $H$ and initial state $e$ held fixed.
Thus, $\mathcal{L}_{H_\phi,\beta}$ is the generator of $Y_t(e)$, and hence $Y_t(e)$ is Glauber dynamics for the gauge-transformed Hamiltonian $H_\phi$ at inverse temperature $\beta$, initialized at $Y_0=e$.
